_about: Reader-facing plain-English `plain` text seeded into the cpl_memory Supabase table for the 📄 Report ('Everything We Know') view. Keyed by slug. Applied by Sky10men (2026-07-25) via a guarded UPDATE ... WHERE plain IS NULL (idempotent, never clobbers a human/curator edit). The terse summary/detail stay the curator+AI surface; `plain` is the non-techie briefing sentence, with an example where the summary is jargon-heavy. Full context: docs/kb-notes/adr-unified-memory-table.md, docs/memory/cpl_memory.md.

plain.d-mem-corroboration-gate: When a Claude session records something new in this memory, it's marked 'proposed' until a second source backs it up — another session, a written-up note, or Sam's checkmark. Only backed-up entries are trusted and shown by default. (It's the same 'get a second opinion' rule we use for course data.)
plain.d-mem-per-org-rls: As the platform starts serving teams beyond CPL (Curriculum & Instruction, CIP, and others), each team's private data has to be genuinely walled off in the database before those teams come aboard — not just visually separated the way it is today. Building that wall early is far easier than retrofitting it later.
plain.d-mem-retrieval-first: This memory is built to be searched, not scrolled. We keep the main list short and curated so it stays useful, and a separate behind-the-scenes log keeps the full history. (A giant scrollable list would just become the same haystack this was meant to replace.)
plain.d1: In new writing the program is the 'CPL Initiative' — never the 'MAP Initiative.' And 'Military Articulation Platform' is used only when telling the 2017 origin story, never for what the platform is today.
plain.d2: TOP codes (the state's subject-area codes on courses) used to decide things like a course's discipline. Because faculty enter them inconsistently, we demoted them to a tie-breaker that only counts when another signal agrees. Reassuringly, making this change didn't alter a single one of our 146 established discipline names.
plain.d3: The Activities tab was reorganized to match the real CPL Workplan's four Activities, and a leftover phantom 'Activity 5' was removed.
plain.d4: GitHub is set up so Claude sessions can merge their own finished work once the automated checks pass, instead of waiting on a manual step — this is why work here ships quickly.
plain.f1: When counting the official statewide credit agreements, use only the rows the data marks as truly statewide ('CCC'). Copies that individual colleges adapted also carry that tag, so lumping them together would over-count. Example: filter to the statewide-flagged rows rather than trying to remove duplicates afterward.
plain.f2: Every course needs one shared reference ID so colleges can tell they're talking about the same course. We use the official state IDs (C-ID / CCN) wherever they exist, and only mint our own placeholder ID (an 'M-ID') for courses that don't have one yet.
plain.f3: The test for whether two courses are 'the same' for credit purposes is simple: would you make a student who passed one retake the other? If not, they're equivalent. This — not whether their subject codes match — is the lens behind every merge decision.
plain.f4: Our 'eligible' label really means 'this credit has a statewide agreement behind it' — it does not mean 'listed on the public statewide CPL webpage.' Example: the Paramedic License credit shows as local here even though people might expect it to count as statewide.
plain.f5: When we need Sam to settle tricky judgment calls, a few carefully chosen examples at a time works far better than dumping thousands of cases on him at once — he'll disengage from the firehose but happily rule on a short, well-framed batch.
plain.f6: CPL 'units' can overstate things because one credential can cover several courses (four courses might all map to a single certification area). So we report course counts as the measure of coverage, not unit totals.
plain.f7: Claude sessions can't reach the database directly — every read and write has to go through a specific set of connector tools. A normal direct connection attempt simply fails.
plain.oh1: The MAP platform launched in 2017 as the 'Military Articulation Platform.' Today it's the 'Mapping Articulated Pathways (MAP) platform' — the old military name is used only when recounting that history.
plain.oh2: AB 123, signed into law in July 2025, is the state law that gives the CPL Initiative its footing.
plain.oh3: CPL stands for Credit for Prior Learning. The CPL Initiative is run by the California Community Colleges Chancellor's Office, and the software behind it is the MAP platform.
plain.oh4: Vision 2030 is the community colleges' statewide master plan; the CPL Initiative is one of the efforts that helps deliver it.
plain.oh5: The live student and savings figures on our dashboards come from the state's MAP CPL Insights Dashboard, pulled automatically each day. Those headline numbers are always fetched fresh, not stored in this memory.
plain.m-mem-loop-closed: This memory now keeps itself up to date: at each regular project 'checkpoint,' the working session records what it learned — so the store maintains itself instead of relying on someone to remember to update it.
plain.m1: Our rulebook for deciding when two courses are the same passed its quality check — it matched Sam's own judgment about 93–95% of the time, good enough to rely on.
plain.m2: We stopped depending on the old master Excel spreadsheet — the daily process no longer writes to it. This was the key step in moving everything onto the live database.
plain.m3: The CPL Initiative secured its 2026–27 funding: $7 million ongoing plus $35 million one-time. This was the headline of Sam's Board of Governors update.
plain.o1: We could automatically flag any course-credit agreement that points at a course a college no longer offers. That would quietly tighten every count across the platform.
plain.o2: The state is moving from the old TOP subject codes to new federal CIP codes (starting fall 2026). That switch is the long-term way out of the TOP-code unreliability problem — we'll treat CIP with the same caution until it proves itself.
plain.p1: The file that tracks daily KPI history can't skip a day. If it does, the 'change since yesterday' figure quietly compares against the wrong day. Fix: fill any missed day with an estimated placeholder.
plain.p2: Never force-overwrite the main code branch — the public website is served straight from it, and the daily automation and other sessions are all working against it at the same time.
plain.p3: Never let a TOP subject code alone decide a course's discipline or identity. Faculty enter them loosely (about half of our merged courses have mismatched TOP codes), so always require a second signal that agrees.
plain.p4: When reading from the database, always page through the results if there could be more than 1,000 — the database silently returns only the first 1,000, in no particular order. Skipping this once made already-saved work look unsaved.
plain.p5: Our 'hide this section' feature has a trap: the Word-export step temporarily un-hides everything to flatten the document, so a section hidden the normal way pops back into the export. Fix: hide it with a special marker the export knows to strip out.
plain.p6: A login token can look valid but actually be expired, so a save silently fails while appearing to succeed. Fix: refresh the token right before every save.
plain.p7: When we renumber course IDs, every related lookup file has to be renumbered too. Skipping one silently breaks the links — one past miss quietly cut more than half of a body of evidence before anyone noticed.
plain.pr1: The dashboard rebuilds itself every day from a generator program, overwriting large parts of the page. So changes have to be made in the generator, not by hand-editing the page (hand edits get wiped the next morning) — and two copies of the page must be kept identical.
plain.pr2: When adding a site-wide color or a hand-built tab, the change has to be made in both copies of the main page, or the two drift apart. (Injecting a tab's styling from its own script avoids having to touch both.)
plain.pr3: When a public-facing term or field is renamed, it has to be updated in six places — the three report generators, the Word-document footers, a settings row, and the public knowledge base — or the old name creeps back into some outputs.
plain.pr4: When course IDs are renumbered, every file and database table that references them has to be renumbered in the same pass — with a dry run first, a saved before→after map, and all of it done inside a single daily window so nothing is left half-changed.
plain.pr5: When a Workplan Activity or Project is renamed or renumbered, four things have to move with it — including a behind-the-scenes link table that was missed last time and left a stale 'Activity 5' showing on one tab.
plain.pr6: Running a project 'checkpoint' means refreshing a fixed set of memory files so the next session can pick up cleanly — the project's rulebook, the reference docs, the to-do feed, the handoff note, and this memory store.
plain.q-mem-measure-pain: Before building a heavyweight 'audit everything we might have missed' feature, first measure whether sessions actually struggle to get oriented today. If that pain is rare, the simpler pieces we already have are enough — and 'measure before you build' is Sam's own rule.
plain.q1: Open question: should every curation tab require the shared team password, or should the more sensitive ones stay behind a tighter personal invite link? The team password is easier and opens access wider; the invite link gives tighter control. This will likely be decided tab by tab.
plain.r-mem-audit-small-n: The experimental 'find what's missing' audit only works at small scale right now — the simple duplicate-detection breaks past a few hundred entries, and sweeping the whole archive is near today's cost limit. Lesson: don't over-invest in it; the real value is flagging contradictions in the curated layer.
plain.r-mem-corpus-not-truth: Our pile of past notes and handoffs is a sediment of stale, sometimes-contradictory, half-finished thoughts. 'Close every gap against those notes' would import dead ideas. We only want what's durable, still true, and not already captured.
plain.r-mem-curation-bottleneck: The real limit on this system is human review time, which doesn't grow as the data does. So we minimize what needs a person: sessions back each other up automatically, only genuine contradictions go to Sam, and it's fine if some entries stay 'proposed' forever.
plain.r1: This memory and the checkpoint notes sync into Sam's private vault with no review step, so they must never contain secrets or personal data, and must never flow to the public knowledge base except through the deliberate, human-reviewed path.
plain.r2: Right now the different team 'sites' (CPL, C&I, and so on) are only a visual switch — they all unlock the same underlying data. Real per-team data separation has to happen before we truly onboard a second team.
plain.r3: Public student-impact counts must always be shown as aggregates, with small groups (fewer than 2) suppressed, to protect privacy. Don't let that guard slip when the export changes.
plain.w1: When Sam gives the go-ahead, run the prepared reorganization of the 2,364 English-as-a-Second-Language courses into Beginning / Intermediate / Advanced, keeping Citizenship, Vocational-ESL, and transfer-level courses separate.
plain.w2: Run the next big batch of course-grouping decisions — 2,000 courses that appear at multiple colleges are staged and ready to work through.
